# Introduction

Young people today come of age within a distinctive tension. On one side stands the meritocratic promise: the assurance, relayed most insistently through schooling, that effort and talent determine life chances and that education is the legitimate route to a better future [@vandewerfhorst_meritocracy_2024]. On the other side stands the world young people actually inhabit, in which inequality has widened, opportunity structures have become more precarious, and the weight of family wealth and social connections on life outcomes is increasingly difficult to ignore [@bourdieu_reproduction_1990; @goudeau_hidden_2017a; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. Youth studies scholarship has long argued that this configuration produces a characteristic predicament: young people experience collective, structural constraints yet are encouraged to interpret their trajectories in individualized terms [@furlong_young_2007], holding onto narratives of hard work and self-improvement even as austerity and stratification undermine the conditions for their fulfillment [@allen_top_2016]. How young people resolve this gap is not only a question about their educational experience; it is a question about their formation as citizens. Beliefs about whether success is earned or inherited underpin how young people judge inequality, whom they hold responsible for it, and what they come to expect from institutions — orientations that constitute the groundwork of civic and political life [@resh_sense_2014; @castillo_socialization_2024].

Schools occupy a privileged place in this process, and in a double sense: they are simultaneously the primary site of meritocratic socialization and a foundational arena of citizenship formation. On the first front, they promote meritocracy as a cultural ideal while institutionalizing it as lived experience through grading, tracking, and selection [@traini_stratification_2022; @darnon_where_2018], making merit visible and consequential during precisely the years when reasoning about justice and fairness becomes more sophisticated [@henry_development_2006]. On the second, the sense of justice young people develop in school does not stay in school: perceptions of fair or unfair treatment within educational institutions are associated with civic attitudes, social trust, and confidence in institutions more broadly [@resh_sense_2014; @resh_sense_2018a]. Young people who believe that effort and talent determine outcomes tend to read success and failure in individual terms, with consequences that extend from how they legitimate inequality to their support for redistribution and their orientation toward collective action [@castillo_socialization_2024; @weinberg_countrylevel_2021]. Yet the same institutions expose them daily to evidence that outcomes are shaped by family background and connections, so that meritocratic ideals and structural awareness develop side by side rather than in sequence.

A growing body of evidence suggests that young people rarely resolve this tension by choosing one side of it. Even those who recognize that wealth and contacts shape outcomes may simultaneously endorse meritocracy as a normative ideal, a configuration the literature describes as dual consciousness [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. This matters because the stakes are civic as much as attitudinal: beliefs about merit are associated, among students, with weaker support for equity-oriented interventions and stronger legitimation of inequality, and among the adults around them, with competitive classroom practices and lower demand for redistributive policy [@batruch_belief_2022; @castillo_socialization_2024; @darnon_where_2018; @darnon_competitive_2023; @wiederkehr_belief_2015]. Yet whether these consequences attach to what young people perceive, to what they prefer, or to how they judge privilege specifically is something existing research has rarely been able to establish — largely because it has treated belief in meritocracy as a single attitude that young people either absorb or reject. A young person who perceives that only connections and wealth get ahead, but insists that effort and talent should determine outcomes, is not disengaged or fatalistic: they hold a normative demand for fairness that the system is failing to meet. Approaches that collapse merit and privilege into opposite ends of a single scale erase this profile by design, misreading critical awareness as disbelief — with the consequence that an emerging civic claim about justice can be mistaken for withdrawal from the meritocratic ideal altogether.

This article examines how young people structure and revise these orientations as they move through schooling. It asks, first, whether young people differentiate between meritocratic and privilege-based accounts of success, and between descriptive judgments of how rewards are allocated and normative judgments of how they should be — or whether these collapse into a single pro- or anti-meritocratic stance. Second, it asks how these orientations develop across adolescence: whether they are stable within individuals over time, and whether accumulated school experience reshapes not just the level of young people's belief in meritocracy but the very meaning they attach to claims like "effort is rewarded." To answer these questions rigorously, we build on the multidimensional framework of Castillo et al. [-@castillo_multidimensional_2023] — which distinguishes perceptions from preferences, and merit from privilege, yielding four analytically distinct orientations — and subject it to formal tests of longitudinal and cross-cohort measurement equivalence.

Measurement invariance is treated here not as a technical formality but as substantively informative: establishing it within students over time is what licenses interpreting observed change as genuine attitudinal development rather than shifting item interpretation [@putnick_measurement_2016; @vandeschoot_editorial_2015], while its absence across school stages is itself a finding about how educational experience transforms the interpretive frames young people bring to meritocratic claims. We pursue these questions with two-wave panel data (2023–2024) on Chilean students aged 11 to 16, drawn from a panel study of young people's beliefs about meritocracy, inequality, and citizenship, and spanning primary and secondary school stages. Chile offers a strategic setting: its educational system combines intense market competition, early tracking, and explicit meritocratic discourse [@castillo_socialization_2024; @valenzuela_socioeconomic_2013] with persistent socioeconomic inequality and a deeply marketized welfare regime [@ferre_welfare_2023]. It is also a country where the legitimacy of that arrangement has been openly contested by young people themselves, from the student movements of the 2000s onward — a reminder that how youth judge the fairness of educational rewards can become consequential for democratic life. This is not a peripheral configuration but an increasingly common one, shared across Latin America and emerging in European and East Asian systems undergoing marketization [@busemeyer_skills_2014; @liu_does_2025]. Chile thus offers a particularly clear window onto a general phenomenon: how young people internalize, question, or reconcile the meritocratic promise with the reality of privilege — and the patterns identified here are likely to travel to other highly stratified contexts where that promise and that reality visibly collide.

In what follows, we review theoretical and empirical work on how young people encounter and interpret meritocracy in school settings, present the study's methodology and results, and discuss what the findings imply for understanding young people's formation as citizens in unequal educational systems — showing that they are not passive recipients of meritocratic ideology but active interpreters of institutional narratives about fairness, whose recognition of privilege can sharpen, rather than extinguish, their demand that rewards should follow merit.
